# Logs, metrics, limits, graceful drain, deploying the binary

---

A WebC app deploys as **one binary and one directory**. There is no runtime to install, no node_modules,
no `PATH` to arrange for a second interpreter: the server is a static-ish C binary, the browser half is a
`.wasm` file it serves, and the assets are the files you wrote.

```sh
webc build --release      # .webc/app, .webc/app.wasm
webc deploy               # whatever `webc.json` says: a tarball, a directory, a container
```

## What is in the build

| Artifact | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `.webc/app` | the server binary: routes, database, views, the SSE links |
| `.webc/app.wasm` | the browser half — only when `webc.json` has a `client` list |
| `public/` | served as-is by `mw_static`, with cache headers |
| `partials/` | authored HTML included by name (`partial("site/head")`), read once at first use |
| `migrations/` | applied at boot, in filename order |

`webc size` reports what each one costs and refuses to guess; `make budget` in the framework repo is
the same number as a gate.

## The three ways to run it

```sh
./.webc/app                              # foreground
PORT=8080 DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pw@localhost:5432/app ./.webc/app
webc serve                               # a release build, served the way a deployment is
```

`webc serve` is the useful one in front of people: gzip on, byte ranges answered, graceful drain on
SIGTERM (in-flight requests finish, streams are closed with a frame the client understands), and the
dev reloader off.

## The ops files: `webc deploy --pack`

The binary is the whole deploy; the files around it are the same in every app except for the name
and the port. The lines that are *not* the same are the ones a copy-paste from a blog gets wrong:

```sh
webc deploy --pack docker,fly,systemd,caddy,nginx   # or: --pack all
```

writes, into `dist/`, the ritual stamped from the manifest it just built:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Dockerfile` | the image around the binary. The base is an `ARG`, not a choice — a base image is a promise about someone else's machine |
| `fly.toml` | fly.io: the port, HTTPS, and a note on why a page with streams wants `min_machines_running = 1` |
| `<name>.service` | a hardened systemd unit: `DynamicUser`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, and the one `ReadWritePaths=` a sqlite file needs |
| `Caddyfile.webc` | the proxy in front — `flush_interval -1` is the line a live page cannot live without |
| `nginx-webc.conf` | the same for nginx: `proxy_buffering off`, a read timeout in hours, the websocket headers |
| `DEPLOY.md` | what each file is and the commands that use it |

The files are the app's the moment they land: edit them, commit them, diff them on the next deploy.
No pack writes an *active* healthcheck — the health route is a convention the app implements (below),
not something the framework serves, and a probe that works in the template and fails on the platform
is worse than none.

## CI: `webc ci`

The gate the docs promise, as a workflow:

```sh
webc ci            # .github/workflows/webc.yml
webc ci --gitlab   # .gitlab-ci.yml
```

It runs `webc check` and `webc test`, attaches a `dist/` artifact on tags, adds the wasi-sdk step by
itself when the app has a client half — and pins the framework with one `WEBC_REF` at the top, the
way any dependency is pinned. Bumping it is an edit the app makes deliberately.

## Configuration

Environment first, then a JSON file, then the default — and the model is the schema for the file, so a
typo in `config.json` is a startup error naming the field rather than a value that silently did not
apply.

```sh
PORT=8080
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pw@host/app
REDIS_URL=redis://host:6379/0
WEBC_SECRET=<32 bytes, hex>          # signs sessions and cookies
WEBC_LOG=info                        # error|warn|info|debug
WEBC_QUERY_CACHE=1
```

A secret that is missing in production is a refusal to start, not a random key per boot — the failure
mode of the latter is sessions that log everyone out on every deploy.

## Health, metrics, and looking inside

```sh
curl localhost:8080/health       # liveness: the route every `webc new` scaffold ships
curl localhost:8080/readyz       # readiness: the database and Redis, if configured
curl localhost:8080/metrics      # Prometheus text format
```

`/health` is app code every scaffold carries (`GET("/health") { return res_text(200, "ok"); }` is
the whole probe), and `/readyz` is the same idea for the database and Redis, by hand where an app
wants it. `/metrics` and `/debug` are the framework's. Point a platform's probe at a route the app
actually serves: the deploy packs ship no active healthcheck for exactly this reason, and a probe
that works in a template and fails on the platform is worse than none.

The metrics are the ones that matter under load, not a generic set: request counts by route and status,
latency histograms, the database pool (open, waiting, refused), the scheduler (tasks runnable, parked),
the query cache (hit, miss, bypassed) and the room table.

`/debug` (behind `WEBC_DEBUG=1`) adds the request log with timings, the route table, the migrated
schema, and a CPU sampler that names the function a slow request was in.

## Behind a proxy

The framework reads `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` only when `WEBC_TRUST_PROXY=1`; that is
the setting that makes rate limits and `peer` mean the client rather than the proxy. Cookies are
`Secure` and `SameSite=Lax` when the request arrived as HTTPS.

```c
// src/main.c — the middleware a deployment adds; the framework installs the rest
#include <webc/server.h>
#include <webc/gzip.h>

void webc_boot(void) {
  // the CSP: the default policy, or the parts of it this deployment changes
  const char *img[] = {"'self'", "data:", "https://cdn.example.com"};
  webc_use(mw_headers((HeadersCfg){.img_src = img, .img_src_n = 3,
                                   .extra = "upgrade-insecure-requests"}));
  webc_use(mw_compress());         // before anything that answers
  // cancels the request's context and the query in flight
  webc_use(mw_timeout_ms(5000));
  webc_use(mw_recover());          // a panic is a 500, not a lost connection
}
```

Order matters in both directions: compression wraps whatever answers after it, and the timeout has
to be inside the headers so the 504 it writes carries them. What is *not* in that function is
already there: `webc_main()` calls `webc_install_default_middleware()` after `webc_boot()`, so the
request id, the logging, the panic recovery, the body limit, the static files, the document pass
and the 404 page are the framework's, and the app's middleware — registered first — wraps all of
it. Two of the calls above are the framework's own defaults, named here because this deployment
puts them in a particular place: a middleware whose name is already in the chain is not
installed twice, so `mw_compress()` and `mw_recover()` are *this* app's, at *this* position, and
there is still exactly one of each. That is also how `mw_headers()` above becomes the policy
instead of a second header beside `webc.json`'s.

Two keys in `webc.json` cover what would otherwise need C: `"csp"` for the policy a project without its
own `mw_headers()` gets, and `"not_found"` for the page a browser gets for a URL nobody routed.

## Databases in production

- **sqlite** is a real choice for a single-node app: `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` is set for you, and
  a write transaction is a file lock rather than a network hop.
- **postgres** speaks the wire protocol directly — no `libpq`, no connection-string quirks — and its
  socket parks like every other fd, so a slow query holds a connection rather than a processor.
- Migrations run at boot. In a multi-instance deploy, run them once (`webc migrate up`) and let the
  instances boot against the migrated schema; `webc check` compares models to schema and names drift.

## The size gate

Byte budgets are part of the build, not a review topic:

```console
$ webc size
  app        .webc/app         1.4 MB
  wasm       .webc/app.wasm    194 KB   (63.5 kB gzip)
  public     public/           12 KB
```

`webc size --modules` builds a probe per standard-library module, so "what does `table.h` cost me" has
an answer instead of an opinion. `make budget` fails the build when a number grows past its limit, which
is why the framework's own floor has stayed where it is.

## A checklist

1. `webc check` clean — build, tests, doctor, boot, schema, routes.
2. `partials/` shipped beside `public/` — a partial is read from disk at runtime, and a
   missing one renders as nothing (one warning in the log, nothing on the page). `webc check`
   catches a name with no file before you deploy, not after.
2. `WEBC_SECRET` set, and different from the dev one.
3. `WEBC_TRUST_PROXY=1` if anything sits in front.
4. `webc migrate up` run (or boot migrations enabled) before traffic.
5. `/readyz` wired into the platform's health check, `/metrics` into its scraper.
6. `SIGTERM` handled — `webc serve` already drains; make sure your platform sends it.

- Reference [§15 Ops](../reference/ops.html) and [§14 The CLI](../reference/the-cli.html).
- [Testing](../guides/testing.html) — what `webc check` runs before any of this.


<!-- docs/reference.md: 15. Ops -->

- Logs: `log_info("request", { "path", req->path }, { "status", ... })`. Text by
  default, JSON with `WEBC_LOG=json`; level from `WEBC_LOG_LEVEL`.
- Metrics: `metrics_counter_inc`, `metrics_observe`; `/metrics` in Prometheus format
  when `WebcOptions.metrics` is set. The server exports `webc_conns`,
  `webc_tasks`, `webc_requests_total` and the connection-close counters
  `webc_conn_closed_eof_total` (the client closed: normal keep-alive end),
  `webc_conn_close_idle_total`, `webc_conn_close_partial_total` (a request was
  cut short) and `webc_conn_read_error_total` (a read failed on our side — the
  one counter that should stay at zero).
- `/debug` reports heap, arenas, tasks and route count; `/debug/cpu?ms=2000` runs the
  sampling profiler for one window and prints a flat profile, and `webc_profile_start()`
  / `webc_profile_stop()` / `webc_profile_report()` do it from code. The sampler
  signals every process thread — including threads the runtime does not own — from a
  dedicated thread, and never itself.
- Limits, all answerable: `WebcOptions{ .max_body, .max_header_bytes, .header_timeout_ms,
  .max_conns, .max_multipart_parts, .max_multipart_bytes, .max_json_depth }`. A body
  over the limit is a 413, headers over the limit a 431, JSON nested deeper than 256 a
  400 that says so.
- Multipart (`<webc/multipart.h>`): `multipart_parse()` plus
  `model_from_multipart()`, so a form with a file lands in the same model as one
  without. Part and byte limits are arguments.
- Redis and the query cache add their counters to the same list (§9d): `webc_cache_*` for what
  the cache did and `webc_redis_*` for what the wire did. `WEBC_TRACE_CACHE=1` prints one line
  per statement (`[cache] select … -> hit`), `WEBC_TRACE_DB=1` prints the statements themselves.
- Budgets are a gate: `make budget` measures SPEC §10 and exits non-zero on a miss (SSR ≥ 100k
  req/s, 1 KB JSON ≤ 1 µs, patch ≤ 0.2 ms, wasm hello ≤ 24 KiB gzip, serve binary ≤ 460 KiB, cold
  build ≤ 1500 ms). The serve binary's line moved from 400 KiB to 460 KiB when Redis and the
  cache became part of it — hello measured 456 544 B on the machine this was written
  on; `make redis-test` runs the client and the cache against a real `redis-server`.
- Shutdown: SIGINT/SIGTERM stop accepting, drain for `drain_ms`, then exit.

---



<!-- docs/reference.md: 16. Limits and deviations -->

These are measured facts, not guesses:

1. **No nested functions.** C23 removed them, so `routes()` cannot contain `GET(...)`.
   Routes are file-scope macros; grouping is done with path prefixes and per-route
   middleware (`GET_MW`).
2. **Bare qualifier flags are invalid C.** `.required` is a syntax error; write
   `.required = true`. There are no token-pasting macros named `required`/`max`, because a
   macro that turns a field into a flag cannot be read back by the compiler's own message.
3. **`state(...)` shadows `state(2)`** in any translation unit that includes
   `<webc/web.h>`; `select(...)` shadows `select(2)` the same way, and that one predates
   it. Include the system headers first. Neither is a problem in a translation unit that
   does not call the POSIX function — and a file that does can call `select_wait` (see
   `task.h`) or keep the system header in its own translation unit.
4. **No guard page on task stacks.** `mprotect(PROT_NONE)` on one page of an anonymous
   mapping makes its neighbours SIGBUS on Darwin (verified with isolated repros), so
   overflow detection is by fault, not by message. A canary at the stack base fires
   falsely on every task because Darwin's ucontext writes its own frames there.
5. **Redis is one server, one database, one process pool.** No Sentinel, no Cluster, no
   `MOVED` redirection, no `SCAN`-driven invalidation: the query cache's counter keys and entries
   assume a single server everybody shares. A Cluster deployment is a different client, not
   a configuration of this one.
6. **TLS is a build feature, off by default.** `-DWEBC_TLS=openssl` (OpenSSL headers
   and libraries; `make tls-test`) enables `res_tls`/`tls_connect`. A build without it
   refuses to start when a listener is configured for TLS instead of serving plaintext
   on a port someone believes is encrypted. Postgres has no TLS, so `sslmode` is not
   implemented.
7. **The wasm target needs wasi-sdk** (~170 MB, a separate download; `webc doctor`
   reports whether it found it). The browser half has no threads, no filesystem and no
   SQL: `include/webc/web.h` is the subset it compiles — core, collections,
   models, JSON, signals, DOM. Verified end to end in Chrome: render, keyed list
   add/remove/toggle, two-way bound input, SSR markup hydrated in place.
8. **Postgres and MySQL are wired and tested** — `make pg-test` starts
   `postgres:16-alpine`, `make mysql-test` starts `mysql:8`, each runs the same suite across
   every driver, and each removes its container. Postgres was untested for most of this build;
   the SQL lexer and the driver twins were found by running it. Only PG16 and
   MySQL 8 are tested — MariaDB gets the same protocol but not its own run, there is no
   `PREPARE` reuse on the postgres side, and there is no pool-exhaustion test for either.
   The MySQL driver has no RSA public-key exchange, so `sha256_password` and
   `caching_sha2_password`'s full authentication need TLS.
9. **A component instance costs 56 B, and `comp()` is opt-in.** One heap `WInst` (24 B) and one
   table slot (32 B) per instance *drawn*, whether or not it reads state; a part called without
   `comp()` pays nothing and shares its position's state (§11d). The 20 000-row table with a
   component per row is therefore still the wrong shape — per-row state is the same arithmetic.
10. **`wcomp_render` re-renders the whole view and diffs.** That is component-level
   reactivity, not per-node: the DOM writes are minimal, the C work is not. §12j's live
   bindings are the per-node half — a leaf the view declares once — but they do not make a
   *structural* change cheap, and they do not raise the 20 000-op mount budget (§16.8).

11. **`webc_serve` runs one worker per core by default** (`cpus = 0` → the online
   processor count, capped at 64; set `cpus = 1` to force a single worker). A task
   may be resumed on a different worker than it started on, so request state and
   the current arena travel with the task, never in a thread-local
   (`webc_req_current()`, `wtask_local()`, and the scope accessors below). Measured with
   `make load` on a 10-core machine: 16 780 req/s of SSR HTML at 16 keep-alive
   connections and 12 112 req/s of one-request-per-connection churn, zero errors
   and no leaked connections or tasks over ~260 000 requests. The bugs that had
   to be fixed first are in `findings/scheduler-and-server-bugs.md`.

12. **Request state is task-local, not thread-local.** If you add an API that
   needs "the current request", the markup build in progress or a per-request
   arena, use the task-local accessors (`webc_req_current()`, `wbuild_current()`,
   and the scope arena the framework installs) — never an arena of your own. A
   `_Thread_local` there is a bug: many tasks share a worker thread, and a task
   that parks resumes on another one. `wbuild_current()` cost a real outage —
   `examples/todo` reads the database *inside* its view, the task parked there,
   and every worker began answering 500 "el() outside a build"; one render then
   dereferenced the null and the process died with SIGSEGV at address 72.

13. **A request allocates nothing that outlives it.** The body, headers, params
    and rows live in the request arena; the render's component (three arenas and
    a command buffer) is destroyed before the response is written; a log line
    allocates nothing at all. Measured: `/metrics` `webc_heap_bytes` is byte-for-byte
    identical before and after 130 000 SSR-with-database requests, and 95 000
    text requests; `webc_arena_bytes` is flat. RSS settles around 11 MB on that
    workload (allocator retention, not growth). Benchmarks print `B/op` for exactly
    this reason: it read 3 200 B/op the hour it was added.
14. **`arena_destroy` gives back what it took.** `wm_stats().arena_live` counts
    chunks that exist, not reservations. Double-counting and keeping the reservation of an
    arena that never allocated is how `/metrics` comes to report 9 GB of live arenas after
    300 000 requests.
15. **`webc_test_request()`'s `Response` lives until the next call** on that
    thread: the helper resets a per-thread arena instead of allocating one per
    call (which leaked 64 KB per request in a loop). Copy what you keep — the
    suites in `examples/` show the pattern.
